newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian troops stop Rwandan refugees fleeing.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian troops stop Rwandan refugees fleeing.

text.p: An estimated 300,000 Rwandan refugees trekked back towards their camps near Tanzania's border with Rwanda on Friday after troops stopped them fleeing into the bush.
Heavily-armed Tanzanian troops surrounded Benaco camp, the largest in Tanzania, after thousands of refugees broke through a cordon of stick-wielding troops to get back to the camp.
Soldiers beat some with sticks but gave up trying to stop the flow when it was clear they had been overrun.

Aid workers expected refugees to be held in Benaco, 17 km (10 miles) from the Rwandan border, and in its satellite camp Musuhura Hill overnight before an expected mass movement under control of police and troops back to Rwanda on Saturday.
Lennart Kotsalainen, acting head of the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) in Tanzania, later told reporters Tanzanian authorities had told UNHCR no refugees would be allowed to remain in the camps.
Asked whether this meant that all the Rwandan refugees would soon be ordered back to Rwanda by Tanzanian authorities, UNHCR senior official Anne Willem Bijleveld said: "I would think so."
"The operation is now completely in the hands of the Tanzanian military," added Bijleveld.
UNHCR officials denied earlier reports that some 5,000 Hutu refugees crossed into Rwanda during the confusion on Friday when the refugees burst out of their camps and trekked off away from Rwanda.
They said only 1,463 voluntarily returned, bringing the total number to go back since Thursday last week to 7,224.

Up to half-a-million Rwandan and Burundian refugees trekked away from their camps and the border on Friday to avoid being repatriated by the end of the month, a deadline set by Tanzania's government and UNHCR on Thursday last week.

But confronted by roadblocks manned by Tanzanian troops, a vast tide of refugees turned back to their camps, only to find they had been sealed off by troops who at one point fired tear gas canisters and shots in the air to keep them on the road.
UNHCR officials said most who had fled were returning towards the camps and put the number at some 350,000. They said troops knew where the others were.
Many Hutu refugees said they fear reprisals or punishment for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis if they return to Rwanda but some others said they would return if they had no choice.
Refugees who wanted to sit down were told to keep moving but the troops were usually good-natured and did not menace them.
Refugees started leaving the camps last Sunday, saying they were on a marathon trek to asylum in Kenya or as far south as Malawi, 850 km (530 miles) away, to avoid being forced home.
"Go back to the camps and you will get fed. We don't want you here. We want you to go back," Tanzanian army Colonel Urbano Nguvumali told refugees on the road as they were turned around.

The exodus had threatened a repeat of events in Zaire in November when over half-a-million Rwandan Hutus fleeing a revolt by Zairean rebels left camps to return to Rwanda while many others fled or were driven by Hutu militia deeper into Zaire.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, appealed to Tanzanian authorities on Thursday to redirect the refugees back towards their camps but without using force.

U.N. officials, who had been in despair at the exodus which they blamed on the Hutu Interahamwe militia intimidating refugees, were delighted as they watched the return flow northwards towards the border.
